'''Sara Jane Rhoads''' (June 1, 1920, [[Kansas City, Missouri]] – May 1, 1993, [[Laramie, Wyoming]]) was an American chemist. She was one of the first women in the United States to become a full professor of chemistry, helped to establish the chemistry department at the [[University of Wyoming]], and was the recipient of the [[American Chemical Society]]'s [[Garvan–Olin Medal]] in 1982.

==Life==

Sara Jane Rhoads was born on June 1, 1920, in [[Kansas City, Missouri]], to Errett Stanley Rhoads and Charlotte Rhoads, née Kraft.<ref name="Obituary">{{cite news |title=Sara Jane Rhoads |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/45809563/obituary-for-sara-jane-rhoads/ |accessdate=15 August 2020 |work=Casper Star-Tribune|place= Casper, Wyoming|page= 12 |date=6 May 1993}}</ref>  She was the youngest of six siblings.<ref name="Smalley"/><ref name="Obituary"/>

Rhoads attended public school in Kansas City. She went to the [[University of Chicago]], where she received her bachelor of science degree in chemistry in 1941.<ref name="Obituary"/><ref name="Papers">{{cite web |title=Sara Jane Rhoads papers, 1938-1994 |url=http://uwcatalog.uwyo.edu/record=b2780924~S3 |website=University of Wisconsin Libraries|publisher=American Heritage Center - Archives |accessdate=15 August 2020}}</ref>

Rhoads worked in the development department of the Lindsay Light and Chemical Company in Chicago between 1941 and 1943. She then taught at the Radford School for Girls in [[El Paso, Texas]] (1943-1944) and at [[Hollins College]] in [[Virginia]] (1944-1945).<ref name="Papers"/>

Rhoads attended [[Columbia University]] in [[New York City]] as a PhD student, receiving her PhD in [[organic chemistry]]<ref name="Obituary"/> under [[William von Eggers Doering]] in 1949.<ref name="Smalley">{{cite book |last1=Smalley |first1=Richard E. |last2=Grenthe |first2=Ingmar |title=Nobel Lectures in Chemistry, 1996-2000 |date=2003 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-9810249595 |pages=81–83 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bnmXGA-pYf8C&pg=PA83 |accessdate=15 August 2020}}</ref>

In September 1948 Sara Jane Rhoads moved to the [[University of Wyoming]], where she worked until her retirement in 1984. In more than 35 years at the university, she devoted herself to teaching and to establishing the chemistry department.<ref name="Obituary"/><ref name="Mole"/>  Between 1956 and 1957 she carried out postdoctoral research in Zurich, Switzerland, working with [[Vladimir Prelog]], who would receive a Nobel Prize in 1975.<ref name="Papers"/>  In 1958, she was one of the first women to become a full professor of chemistry in the United States.<ref name="Obituary"/><ref name="Mole">{{cite web |title=Happy Mole Day! |url=https://ahcwyo.org/2012/10/23/happy-mole-day/ |website=American Heritage Center (AHC) News |accessdate=15 August 2020|date=October 23, 2012}}</ref>  She initiated  the University of Wyoming's undergraduate research program, and served as the department's director from 1967-1968.<ref name="Guide">"Sara Jane Rhoads papers, 1938-1994" in {{cite web |title=Guide to Women's History Resources at the American Heritage Center|page=77 |url=http://www.uwyo.edu/ahc/_files/collection_guides/womenshist_guide_2012_ed_jan_2018.pdf |website=University of Wyoming Libraries }}</ref>

In 1959, Rhoads was the first person at the University of Wyoming to receive  a grant from the [[National Science Foundation]].<ref name="Obituary"/> She and [[Darleane Hoffman]] were the only two women, along with 161 men, who received a Senior Post Doctoral Fellowship from the National Science Foundation between 1956 and 1971.<ref name="Rossiter">{{cite book |last1=Rossiter |volume= 2 |first1=Margaret W. |title=Women Scientists in America: Before Affirmative Action, 1940-1972 |date=1995 |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |location=Baltimore, Maryland |pages=318–319}}</ref> As of 1971 [[N. Rebecca Raulins]] was the only other woman chemist on the University of Wyoming faculty: nonetheless  the university actually ranked higher than most American universities of the time in hiring women faculty.<ref name="Roundtable">{{cite book |last1=Rossiter |first1=Margaret W. |editor= National Research Council (US) |title=Women in the Chemical Workforce: A Workshop Report to the Chemical Sciences Roundtable |chapter=Chapter 1, 1970-2000: A Less Than Golden Age for Women in Chemistry? |date=2000 |publisher=National Academies Press (US) |location=Washington (DC) |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK44846/ |accessdate=15 August 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Few Women in Academia |journal=Chemical & Engineering News |date=May 10, 1971 |volume=49 |issue=19 |page=21|doi=10.1021/cen-v049n019.p021a }}</ref>

Rhoads received the national [[Manufacturing Chemists' Association]] Award for Outstanding College Teaching in 1964, and the George Duke Humphrey Distinguished Faculty Award in 1974.<ref name="Obituary"/>
She received the [[American Chemical Society]]'s [[Garvan–Olin Medal]] in 1982.<ref name="ACS"/><ref name="Garvan"/> The university established the annual Sara Jane Rhoads & Rebecca Raulins Lecture in Organic Chemistry in 1992.<ref name="Papers"/>

Rhoads' nephew [[Richard E. Smalley]] admired her and was inspired by her to pursue a career as a chemist.  He worked in her laboratories in the 1960s. Smalley became a pioneer in the field of [[nanotechnology]] and received the 1996 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] with [[Robert F. Curl]] and [[Harold Kroto]] for the discovery of [[fullerenes]].<ref name="Mole"/><ref name="Smalley"/>

==Awards==
* 1947–1948, [[American Association of University Women]] (AAUW) Fellowship<ref name="Papers"/>
* 1956, NSF Senior Post Doctoral Fellowship, [[National Science Foundation]]<ref name="Papers"/>
* 1964, Award for Outstanding College Teaching,  [[Manufacturing Chemists' Association]]<ref name="Obituary"/><ref name="NYT1964">{{cite news |title=Three Win Chemistry Awards |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/05/04/archives/three-win-chemistry-awards.html |accessdate=15 August 2020 |work=The New York Times |date=May 4, 1964}}</ref>
* 1974, George Duke Humphrey Distinguished Faculty Award<ref name="Obituary"/>
* 1982, [[Garvan–Olin Medal]], [[American Chemical Society]]<ref name="ACS">{{cite web |title=Francis P. Garvan-John M. Olin Medal |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/francis-p-garvan-john-m-olin-medal.html |website=American Chemical Society }}</ref><ref name="Garvan">{{cite web |author=Special Collections and University Archives |title=Finding Aid for MS 678 Garvan Medalists Survey Collection, 1981-2000 |url=http://findingaids.lib.iastate.edu/spcl/manuscripts/MS678.html |website=Iowa State University }}</ref><ref name="Gleiser">{{cite journal |last1=Gleiser |first1=Molly |title=The Garvan women |journal=Journal of Chemical Education |date=December 1985 |volume=62 |issue=12 |pages=1065 |doi=10.1021/ed062p1065|bibcode=1985JChEd..62.1065G }}</ref>
